newsitem.title: CROATIA: Opposition protests poll results in Zagreb.
newsitem.headline: Opposition protests poll results in Zagreb.

text.p: An opposition coalition cried foul on Tuesday at voting returns for the Zagreb city assembly that yielded more seats to Croatia's ruling nationalist party although it got fewer votes than rivals.

A final unofficial count announced by the state electoral commission said the ex-communist Social Democrats (SDP) and the Social Liberals (HSLS) won a combined 36.76 percent of the vote, while the governing Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ) took 35.67 percent.

But the long-ruling HDZ of authoritarian President Franjo Tudjman said on Tuesday that it would get 24 seats in the Zagreb assembly, against 23 for the SDP-HSLS coalition. The HDZ still needs two more seats to cement an absolute majority.
Another three seats were awarded by the HDZ-led commission to the Peasants Party (HSS), which had refused to associate with SDP because of its communist past.
HDZ Zagreb party chairman Zlatko Canjuga claimed the party had posted "a complete and clear" victory in Sunday's polls.
HSLS secretary Karlo Gorinsek shot back: "We (opposition) definitely got more votes. This is a deceit, unless the HDZ has already managed to rig the results.

"The electoral commission procrastinates with publishing official results for Zagreb. They are now flaunting the county and upper House of Counties results (heavily pro-HDZ) and meanwhile they will manipulate results here," he told Reuters.

The HDZ, riding on the "Father-of-the-Nation" charisma of Tudjman, cruised to a renewed absolute majority in 18 of 21 county assemblies. That gave it at least 41 of 68 seats in the Upper House of the parliament.
However, the party appeared to have lost in virtually all major cities, according to the independent weekly Nacional on Tuesday, although final results have yet to be released.
"Croatia has some similarities to Serbia - the ruling party loses towns and wins in rural areas," said political analyst Davor Gjenero.
Serbia's opposition coalition won the capital Belgrade last November and the ruling socialist party refused to recognise its defeat until after three months of street protests.

Zagreb controls most of the country's economy and finance. However, an opposition victory in the city is likely to be only a symbolic defeat for the HDZ, which already got an absolute majority in Zagreb county, a ring around the capital.

The SDP said the sudden reversal of the opposition's fortune in Zagreb resulted from a complicated method of distributing seats accounting for the popular vote of parties that did not clear a five percent threshold for representation.
"This is electoral engineering which suits best the HDZ, that's why they devised it," SDP co-leader Zdravko Tomac said.

The HDZ wasted no time beginning post-electoral manoeuvring by offering "cooperation" to the HSLS and HSS, in a bid to achieve at least a one-seat majority in the assembly by splintering the opposition coalition.
HSS leader Zlatko Tomcic told Reuters the party was "not going to form any coalitions at the moment".

The HDZ lost to a loose seven-party coalition in Zagreb in 1995. But Tudjman, citing "national security" as grounds, vetoed four opposition mayoral nominees and imposed a provisional HDZ city administration.

His move brought accusations of authoritarianism and was condemned in the West. Tudjman argued the HDZ had won a "relative majority" while the opposition was an unstable mishmash of parties ranging from far left to far right.
Former rebel Serbs also completed their first election in post-independence Croatia, judged by the United Nations to be fair despite technical hitches that almost ruined it.

Voting in the Eastern Slavonia enclave, which reverts to Croatian rule this summer after 18 months under U.N. protection, was extended into Monday to make up time for technical delays. One polling station was open even on Tuesday.
Organisational bungling led to misplaced and insufficient ballot forms, halting voting there for hours on Sunday.
The first unofficial results will be released on Wednesday and it was still unknown how many of the eligible 150,000 Serbs had actually voted, the Croatian state news agency HINA said.
The U.N. said its administrator Jacques Klein is expected to proclaim the voting free and fair.
